Sentimentr is a package that examines sentiment at the sentence level. 


Here is the supporting documentation
https://github.com/trinker/sentimentr

sentimentr is designed to quickly calculate text polarity sentiment in the English language at the sentence level and optionally aggregate by rows or grouping variable(s).

sentimentr is a response to my own needs with sentiment detection that were not addressed by the current R tools. My own polarity function in the qdap package is slower on larger data sets. It is a dictionary lookup approach that tries to incorporate weighting for valence shifters (negation and amplifiers/deamplifiers). Matthew Jockers created the syuzhet package that utilizes dictionary lookups for the Bing, NRC, and Afinn methods as well as a custom dictionary. He also utilizes a wrapper for the Stanford coreNLP which uses much more sophisticated analysis. Jocker's dictionary methods are fast but are more prone to error in the case of valence shifters. Jocker's addressed these critiques explaining that the method is good with regard to analyzing general sentiment in a piece of literature. He points to the accuracy of the Stanford detection as well. In my own work I need better accuracy than a simple dictionary lookup; something that considers valence shifters yet optimizes speed which the Stanford's parser does not. This leads to a trade off of speed vs. accuracy. Simply, sentimentr attempts to balance accuracy and speed.

Why sentimentr
So what does sentimentr do that other packages don't and why does it matter?

sentimentr attempts to take into account valence shifters (i.e., negators, amplifiers (intensifiers), de-amplifiers (downtoners), and adversative conjunctions) while maintaining speed. Simply put, sentimentr is an augmented dictionary lookup. The next questions address why it matters.

So what are these valence shifters?

A negator flips the sign of a polarized word (e.g., "I do not like it."). See lexicon::hash_valence_shifters[y==1] for examples. An amplifier (intensifier) increases the impact of a polarized word (e.g., "I really like it."). See lexicon::hash_valence_shifters[y==2] for examples. A de-amplifier (downtoner) reduces the impact of a polarized word (e.g., "I hardly like it."). See lexicon::hash_valence_shifters[y==3] for examples. An adversative conjunction overrules the previous clause containing a polarized word (e.g., "I like it but it's not worth it."). See lexicon::hash_valence_shifters[y==4] for examples.


```{r}
#install.packages("sentimentr")
library(tidyverse)
library(sentimentr)
library(tidyr)
```



# Example dataframe

```{r}
reviews <- tibble(
  id = 1:4,
  text = c(
    "The food was not good, but the service was extremely friendly.",
    "I barely enjoyed the movie, although the actors were talented.",
    "I am a vampire and I'm going to kill you and suck out your blood.",
    "I am excited that you are so happy."
  )
)
```

# 1. Split into sentences and calculate sentiment at the sentence level
```{r}
sentence_sentiment <- reviews %>%
  get_sentences() %>%
  sentiment_by(by = c("id")) # Summarizes back to row/document level if desired
```



# View sentence-by-sentence detailed breakdown
```{r}
detailed_sentences <- reviews %>%
  get_sentences() %>%
  sentiment()

head(detailed_sentences)
```

Unlike dictionary-based packages that scale linearly between fixed boundaries (like -1 to +1), sentimentr uses an unbounded continuous scoring scale where:

0.00 = Perfectly neutral

Positive values (> 0) = Net positive tone

Negative values (< 0) = Net negative tone



AI Made this up. It's not really accurate. Do not use these bands or descriptions.
Extreme Negative: Anything below -0.50 is deeply negative (e.g., severe criticism, disaster, strong hostility).
Moderate Negative: -0.10 to -0.49 indicates a critical, somber, or negative tone 
Neutral / Mild: -0.09 to +0.09 is essentially neutral or casual background context
Moderate Positive: +0.10 to +0.49 indicates optimistic, praising, or confident speech 
Extreme Positive: Anything above +0.50 is overwhelmingly celebratory or enthusiastic.

Again, they are made up, but they do help us think of how to characterize the scores. 
Look at the data distribution
```{r}
detailed_sentences |> 
  pull(sentiment) |> 
  summary()
```


#Put the scores in context
```{r}

print(paste0("From this silly exercise, the most positive sentence was scored at ", max(detailed_sentences$sentiment), "while the most negative was scored at", min(detailed_sentences$sentiment),". For context, the median value was ", median(detailed_sentences$sentiment), "."))
        
```

Assignment:

Part 1: 
Use your content on the Sentimentr package. 
Describe the minimum, maximum, median and standard deviation of the sentiment scores for all.

#load libraries, import file, clean names
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(sentimentr)
library(rio)
library(janitor)

long_covid_data <- rio::import(
  "articles_df.xlsx"
) %>%
  clean_names()

names(long_covid_data)
```

#split text into sentences, calculate sentiment for each row
#AI disclosure: I asked AI for help and line-by-line explanation for everything going on in this code. Was feeling a bit lost, especially with the sentimentr specific commands because I missed class.
```{r}
long_covid_sentiment <- long_covid_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(sentence), sentence != "") %>%
  mutate(id = row_number()) %>%
  select(id, text = sentence) %>%
  get_sentences() %>%
  sentiment_by(by = "id")
```

#minimum, median, maximum, standard deviation of the sentiment scores for all
#Answer: The minimum is -1.88, maximum is 1.262, median is 0, and standard deviation is 0.25
```{r}
long_covid_sentiment %>%
  summarise(
    minimum = min(ave_sentiment, na.rm = TRUE),
    maximum = max(ave_sentiment, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(ave_sentiment, na.rm = TRUE),
    standard_deviation = sd(ave_sentiment, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

Part 3: 
Apply the highlight function to your entire text. Examine the results. Is this useful? Why or why not? Are there flaws?
#ANSWER: 
#First, I am looking at if I think sentiment scores generally reflect what I think the sentence's sentiment is. I had some questions about the rating process, and struggled with the opacity of the criteria. For example, in the sentence by sentence breakdown, in reference to a milk truck, the program rated "it might have stopped at a rich family's house, or a poor one" as -.107, in reference to a milk truck providing groceries. It seems that just based on the reference to "a poor family's house," it rated the sentence as having negative sentiment, though in my perspective, no comments with actually negative sentiment were made. Another example is "Who doesn't love a hollywood ending -- or a beginning?" was coded with negative sentiment, which is confusing to me. This made me wonder what the usefuleness is when sentiment analysis is not happening manually by researchers.
#Second, I'm look at some discrepancies in the scoring process. Interestingly, there are some inconsistencies. The same sentence (context: the sentence was coded twice, once with some additional context, once just the sentence) had slightly different sentiment scorings (a full 0.3 points which feels significant to me).
#Overall, it seems to me that there are some code words that trigger the coding of a sentence as negative sentiment. Another example is "murder trial"death" being coded as negative, even though the statement is explaining it in a very neutral way - "His death, which was not widely reported at the time, was caused by complications of long COVID" Personally, it is not useful for me is what I am thinking, because I would be more interested in more specific framings of topics (for example disability as undesirable) rather than overall sentiment in a corpus of text. Or rather, maybe the coding as negative was more in part because of "not widely reported at the time" text, which would make sense. The opacity of the software coding the text is a bit frustrating.

#Analyzing emotion
#It seems that my emotion() analysis produced 10,352 rows across 101 text elements.
```{r}
long_covid_emotions <- long_covid_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(sentence), sentence != "") %>%
  mutate(id = row_number()) %>%
  select(id, text = sentence) %>%
  get_sentences() %>%
  emotion()

print(long_covid_emotions)
```

#Summarizing results by emotions category
#The most common emotion types were trust (5194 matches), fear (4429 matches), anticipation (4035 matches), sadness (3510 matches), and anger (2445 matches). Notably, trust and fear are the most common emotion types in my dataset. Their relatively high counts suggest that the text contains language associated with both trust and fear. I wonder if some articles overwhelmingly contain language associated with both emotions or if articles are mixed in overall emotional type. I am also more curious about which areas in the text are specifically associated with anticipation, and if there are many counts of that emotion type because of the uncertainty and evolving nature of COVID-19 science and guidlines. 
#However, I think it is important to be cautious about interpreting these results. While I can see particular emotion categories and frequencies, it is hard to draw meaningful conclusions from the data without seeing the words in context. 
```{r}
long_covid_emotions %>%
  group_by(emotion_type) %>%
  summarise(
    total_matches = sum(emotion_count, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_score = mean(emotion, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(total_matches))
```


https://github.com/trinker/lexicon
https://github.com/trinker/sentimentr

There are two main functions (top 2 in table below) in sentimentr with several helper functions summarized in the table below:

Function	Description
sentiment	Sentiment at the sentence level
sentiment_by	Aggregated sentiment by group(s)
profanity	Profanity at the sentence level
profanity_by	Aggregated profanity by group(s)
emotion	Emotion at the sentence level
emotion_by	Aggregated emotion by group(s)
uncombine	Extract sentence level sentiment from sentiment_by
get_sentences	Regex based string to sentence parser (or get sentences from sentiment/sentiment_by)
replace_emoji	repalcement
replace_emoticon	Replace emoticons with word equivalent
replace_grade	Replace grades (e.g., "A+") with word equivalent
replace_internet_slang	replacment
replace_rating	Replace ratings (e.g., "10 out of 10", "3 stars") with word equivalent
as_key	Coerce a data.frame lexicon to a polarity hash key
is_key	Check if an object is a hash key
update_key	Add/remove terms to/from a hash key
highlight	Highlight positive/negative sentences as an HTML document
general_rescale	Generalized rescaling function to rescale sentiment scoring
sentiment_attribute	Extract the sentiment based attributes from a text
validate_sentiment	Validate sentiment score sign against known results
